'''''Bassia scoparia''''' is a large annual herb in the family [[Amaranthaceae]] (''[[sensu lato]]'') native to Eurasia. It has been [[introduced species|introduced]] to many parts of [[North America]],<ref name="plants">[https://plants.usda.gov/DocumentLibrary/plantguide/pdf/pg_basc5.pdf ''Bassia scoparia''.] USDA PLANTS. Retrieved June 16, 2024.</ref> where it is found in grassland, prairie, and desert shrub ecosystems.<ref name="feis">[http://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/forb/kocsco/all.html ''Kochia scoparia''.] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100113160539/http://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/forb/kocsco/all.html |date=January 13, 2010 }} USFS  
Fire Effects Information System.</ref>  Its [[common name]]s include '''summer cypress''',<ref name="feis" /> '''mock-cypress''', '''kochia''', '''belvedere''', '''World's Fair plant''', '''burningbush''',<ref name="plants"/> '''Mexican firebrush''', and '''Mexican fireweed''',<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | accessdate = 24 December 2017}}</ref> with the latter three names referring to the herb's red autumn foliage.

==Description==
The fruit of ''Bassia scoparia'' with the [[Calyx (botany)|calyx]] attached is dull brown, but when hulled, it reveals dull black seeds,<ref name=egginton>{{citation|last=Egginton |first=George E. |author-link=<!--George E. Egginton--> |title=Colorado Weed Seeds |journal=Bulletin - Colorado Agricultural Experiment Station |number=260 |date=January 1921|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mzVLAQAAMAAJ&pg=RA2-PA38 |page=38}}</ref> or dark to blackish-brown seeds in some escaped regions, such as Europe.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Bojnanský |first1=Vít |author1-link=:sk:Vít Bojňanský (botanik) |last2=Fargašová |first2=Agáta |author2-link=<!--Agáta Fargašová--> |title=Atlas of Seeds and Fruits of Central and East-European Flora: The Carpathian Mountains Region |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |year=2007 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5vd_ZE7UDV8C&pg=PA107 |pages=107 |isbn=<!--1402053614, -->9781402053610}}</ref>

The seeds are dispersed by wind and water and are transported when the whole plant detaches and rolls on the wind as a [[tumbleweed]].<ref name="feis" /> The seed does not persist in the [[soil seed bank]], dying within about a year if it fails to germinate.<ref name="feis" />
The species is a [[C4 carbon fixation|C<sub>4</sub>]] plant, specifically of the NADP-ME type.<ref name="kadereit">{{cite journal |last1=Kadereit |first1=Gudrun |first2=Helmut |last2=Freitag |year=2011 |url=http://openurl.ingenta.com/content?genre=article&issn=0040-0262&volume=60&issue=1&spage=51&epage=78 |title=Molecular phylogeny of Camphorosmeae (Camphorosmoideae, Chenopodiaceae): Implications for biogeography, evolution of C<sub>4</sub>-photosynthesis and taxonomy |journal=Taxon |volume=60 |issue=1 |pages=51–78 |doi=10.1002/tax.601006 |bibcode=2011Taxon..60...51K |url-access=subscription }}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Muhaidat R, Sage RF, Dengler NG |title=Diversity of Kranz anatomy and biochemistry in C4 eudicots |journal=American Journal of Botany |volume=94 |issue=3 |pages=362–81 |date=March 2007  |pmid=21636407 |doi=10.3732/ajb.94.3.362}}</ref>
It develops [[herbicide resistance]] unusually quickly,<ref name="Kumar-et-al-2018">{{cite journal|doi=10.1017/wsc.2018.72|journal=[[Weed Science (journal)|Weed Science]]|publisher=[[Weed Science Society of America]]|title=Herbicide-Resistant Kochia (Bassia scoparia) in North America: A Review|date=2018-12-07|last1=Kumar|first1=Vipan|last2=Jha|first2=Prashant|last3=Jugulam|first3=Mithila|last4=Yadav|first4=Ramawatar|last5=Stahlman|first5=Phillip W.|volume=67|pages=4–15|s2cid=91312866|doi-access=free}}</ref> and quadruple-resistant populations have developed in [[North America]].<ref name="Kumar-et-al-2018" />

''Bassia scoparia'' is native to a region ranging from Central Europe to Asia and is now widespread throughout the world. While having a variety of beneficial uses, it is also considered an invasive weed.<ref name="plants"/>
[[File:Outdoor lightning of Bassia scoparia.jpg|thumb|Close-up photo of ''Bassia scoparia'' taken outdoors in natural light. Captured in [[India]]]]

== Taxonomy ==
The species was first published in 1753 by [[Carl Linnaeus]], who named it ''Chenopodium scoparium''. In 1809, it was placed in the  genus ''Kochia'' by [[Heinrich Schrader (botanist)|Heinrich Schrader]]. It was transferred to ''[[Bassia]]'' in 1978 by [[Andrew John Scott (botanist)|Andrew J. Scott]]. ''Kochia'' was included in ''Bassia'' in 2011 following [[phylogenetics|phylogenetic]] studies.<ref name="kadereit" />

==Uses==
This plant is grown as an [[ornamental plant]] as evergreen foliage for landscapes,<ref name=":0">{{cite web |title=Kochia Scoparia |url=http://www.thelovelyplants.com/easy-to-grow-foliage-plant-kochia-scoparia-summer-cypress/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190409035242/http://www.thelovelyplants.com:80/easy-to-grow-foliage-plant-kochia-scoparia-summer-cypresshttps://web.archive.org/web/20190409035242/http://www.thelovelyplants.com:80/easy-to-grow-foliage-plant-kochia-scoparia-summer-cypress |archive-date=2019-04-09 |access-date=2022-06-06 |website=The Lovely Plants}}</ref> as well as for its red fall foliage. It has also been useful in [[erosion]] control on denuded soils.<ref name=casey>{{cite web |last=Casey |first=P.A. |year=2009 |title=Plant guide for kochia (''Kochia scoparia'') |publisher=USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, Kansas Plant Materials Center |location=Manhattan, Kansas |url=https://plants.usda.gov/plantguide/pdf/pg_kosc.pdf}}</ref> It has been suggested as an agent of [[phytoremediation]],<ref name=casey/> because it is a [[hyperaccumulator]] of [[chromium]], [[lead]], [[Mercury (element)|mercury]], [[selenium]], [[silver]], [[zinc]],<ref>{{cite book |last1=McCutcheon |last2=Schnoor |title=Phytoremediation |location=New Jersey |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |year=2003}}{{page needed|date=June 2014}}</ref> and [[uranium]].<ref name=schm>{{cite journal |author=Schmidt U |title=Enhancing phytoextraction: the effect of chemical soil manipulation on mobility, plant accumulation, and leaching of heavy metals |journal=Journal of Environmental Quality |volume=32 |issue=6 |pages=1939–54 |year=2003 |pmid=14674516 |doi=10.2134/jeq2003.1939}}</ref>

===''Tonburi''===
{{Redirect-distinguish|Tonburi|Thonburi (disambiguation){{!}}Thonburi}}
[[File:Tonburi Seed.JPG|alt=Tonburi|thumb|Tonburi]]
In [[Japan]] the dull black seeds are used as a [[Garnish (food)|food garnish]] called {{nihongo|''tonburi''|[[:ja:とんぶり|とんぶり]]|}} ([[Japanese language|Japanese]]).<ref name="dai-nihon"/> Because its texture is similar to [[caviar]], it has been called "land caviar",<ref name="chiba">{{cite book|last=Chiba |first=Machiko |author-link=<!--千葉真知子--> |title=Japanese Dishes for Wine Lovers |location= |publisher=Kodansha International |date=2005 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=La1juytBR0EC&pg=PA117 |page=117 |isbn=<!--4770030037, -->9784770030030}}</ref> "field caviar", and "mountain caviar".<ref name="dai-nihon"/> It is a ''[[chinmi]]'', or delicacy, in [[Akita prefecture]].<ref name="asahi-japan"/><ref name="dai-nihon"/><!--[[Ugo Province]]--> The seed dish is prepared by boiling the seeds for about 30{{spaces}}minutes, soaking them in running water, and rubbing them in the hands to hull them.<ref name="asahi-japan">{{cite book|title=This is Japan |location= |publisher=Asahi Shinbunsha |date=1954 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-iXVAAAAMAAJ&q=tomburi+caviar |page=117}}</ref>

===Traditional medicine===
The seeds are used in [[traditional Chinese medicine]] to help regulate disorders such as [[hyperlipidemia]], [[hypertension]], [[obesity]], and [[atherosclerosis]]. In a study of mice fed a high-fat diet, an extract of the seeds limited obesity.<ref name=han>{{cite journal |vauthors=Han LK, Nose R, Li W |title=Reduction of fat storage in mice fed a high-fat diet long term by treatment with saponins prepared from Kochia scoparia fruit |journal=Phytotherapy Research |volume=20 |issue=10 |pages=877–82 |date=October 2006  |pmid=16892459 |doi=10.1002/ptr.1981|s2cid=25309137 |display-authors=etal}}</ref> They contain [[momordin (saponin)|momordin Ic]], a [[triterpene]] [[saponin]].<ref name=matsuda>{{cite journal |vauthors=Matsuda H, Li Y, Yamahara J, Yoshikawa M |title=Inhibition of gastric emptying by triterpene saponin, momordin Ic, in mice: roles of blood glucose, capsaicin-sensitive sensory nerves, and central nervous system |journal=The Journal of Pharmacology and Experimental Therapeutics |volume=289 |issue=2 |pages=729–34 |date=May 1999  |doi=10.1016/S0022-3565(24)38194-7 |pmid=10215646 |url=http://jpet.aspetjournals.org/cgi/pmidlookup?view=long&pmid=10215646|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

===Foraging===
The plant is a moderately useful [[forage]] for [[livestock]], especially on dry lands.<ref name=rank>{{cite journal |vauthors=Rankins DL, Smith GS, Hallford DM |title=Serum constituents and metabolic hormones in sheep and cattle fed Kochia scoparia hay |journal=Journal of Animal Science |volume=69 |issue=7 |pages=2941–6 |date=July 1991  |doi=10.2527/1991.6972941x |pmid=1885403 |url=http://www.journalofanimalscience.org/cgi/pmidlookup?view=long&pmid=1885403|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The plant contains higher levels of protein and oxalate than most grasses and fodder plants.<ref name=":0" /> However, its use is limited by its [[toxicity]] in large quantities.<ref name="pmid1938652">{{cite journal |vauthors=Rankins DL, Smith GS, Hallford DM |title=Effects of metoclopramide on steers fed Kochia scoparia hay |journal=Journal of Animal Science |volume=69 |issue=9 |pages=3699–705 |date=September 1991  |doi=10.2527/1991.6993699x |pmid=1938652 |url=http://www.journalofanimalscience.org/cgi/pmidlookup?view=long&pmid=1938652|doi-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Livestock ingesting large amounts can experience weight loss, [[hyperbilirubinemia]], [[photosensitization]], and [[polyuria]].<ref name="pmid1885402">{{cite journal |vauthors=Rankins DL, Smith GS, Hallford DM |title=Altered metabolic hormones, impaired nitrogen retention, and hepatotoxicosis in lambs fed Kochia scoparia hay |journal=Journal of Animal Science |volume=69 |issue=7 |pages=2932–40 |date=July 1991  |doi=10.2527/1991.6972932x |pmid=1885402 |url=http://www.journalofanimalscience.org/cgi/pmidlookup?view=long&pmid=1885402|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Brooms ===
The plant's common name in Japan is {{Nihongo||箒木|hahaki-gi}} or {{Nihongo||箒草|hōki-gusa}} which signify 'broom-tree' or 'broom-weed', and it has traditionally been used to make [[broom]]s.<ref name="dai-nihon">{{cite book|author=Dai Nihon Nōkai<!--Agricultural Society of Japan--> |author-link=<!--Dai Nihon Nōkai--> |chapter=Kochia Scoparia |title=Useful Plants of Japan Described and Illustrated |location= |publisher=Agricultural Society of Japan |year=1895 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=g9dBAAAAIAAJ&pg=PA80  |page=80}}</ref><ref name=cranston/>

In [[Serbia]] and Bulgaria,<ref name="hero">{{Cite web|url=https://korovametla.wordpress.com/|title=Hero korova metla 2012|last=|first=|date=|website=|publisher=|language=Serbian|access-date=2017-01-16}}</ref> brooms are produced by simply tying several dried plants of this species together, using the branches as the broom head and the stems as the [[handle]]; this is convenient since the broom does not require a separate handle.<ref name="hero" />

==Culture==

Medieval Japanese legend has it that this broom tree would disappear from sight whenever approached, and [[Sakanoue no Korenori]] wrote a waka poem alluding to this myth.<ref name=cranston>{{cite book|last=Cranston |first=Edwin A. |author-link=Edwin A. Cranston |title=A Waka Anthology: Grasses of remembrance (2 v.) |location= |publisher=Stanford University Press |date=1993 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3RI7XH8bdMoC&pg=PA698 |page=698|isbn=<!--080474825X, -->9780804748254}}</ref>
